KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Paper Plane Target — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches paper plane target — a folding game and a flying game joined at the crease.

What is this?

Paper plane target is an aiming game: fold a plane, then fly it at a target on the floor — a drawn bullseye, a hoop, or a laundry basket.

What does it mean?

A plane is a throw that keeps going after your hand lets go — the folds decide the flight, and every flight teaches the next fold.

What does the child need to know?

You need paper (one sheet per plane), and a target: a paper-plate bullseye on the floor, a hoop, or the basket that lost its socks.

Why this matters

The folding is real craft with a job at the end, and the target gives every flight a story — close miss, bullseye, or the legendary basket landing.

What it teaches

Paper folding (the fine-motor art of exact creases), underarm flight throws, and distance-plus-accuracy aiming.

Words to learn

paperplanefoldcreasethrowflytarget

Say this to your child

“"Fold the corners to the middle — crease it flat! Now stand behind the line, aim the nose at the bullseye, and glide it — smooth and gentle."”

Step by step

  1. Fold the plane: paper in half the long way, open it, fold the two top corners to the middle line, fold the new point down, fold the sides to the middle once more.
  2. Draw a bullseye on paper or put a basket where the floor is clear.
  3. Stand behind the line — three big steps from the target.
  4. Hold the plane under its belly, aim, and let it glide — a smooth push, not a hard slam.
  5. Score it: one point for a close landing, three for the bullseye, five for the basket.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, two paper planes fly toward a red-and-white target on a stand — one plane is close and one is still climbing, because every flight lands somewhere different.

Ask your child

"Which fold made the biggest difference?" "What happens when you throw harder?" "Where should the nose point at the moment you let go?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might name every plane before its first flight, fold a fleet of five and fly them in formation, or adjust the wing tips after every throw like a real test pilot.

Out in the real world

In the UK the same plane is a paper aeroplane — same folds, same flight. Folding planes is a game that travels: one sheet of paper turns any waiting room into a target range.

Try it together

Best of five flights each. Then the engineering round: bend the back edges of the wings up a little, fly again, and see what changed — real aerodynamics, discovered by hand.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we fold first?" (the paper in half, the long way) "Do we slam the plane or glide it?" (glide it — smooth and gentle)
